extracted.intended_audience: graduate/advanced undergraduate students studying algebraic geometry (Math 216)
extracted.subtask_description: Textbook chapter (Vakil) covering regularity of schemes, Bertini's theorem, discrete valuation rings, and the definition/properties of smooth and étale morphisms, with proofs and exercises. Intended as course material and reference for understanding and checking these properties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ways to show Z[i] has dimension 1
rubrics_metrics.description: There are several ways of showing that Z[i] is dimension 1: (i) it is a principal ideal domain; (ii) it is the normalization of Z in the field extension Q(i)/Q; (iii) using Krull’s Principal Ideal Theorem and the fact that dim Z[x] = 2.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use any of the listed approaches. As an application, show that Spec Z[i] is a regular curve; for practice consider the prime (2, 1 + i), which is cut out by 2 and 1 + x in Spec Z[x]/(x^2 + 1). A later simpler approach uses discrete valuation rings (see §12.5.10).

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 12.3.6: Regularity preserved when adjoining a polynomial variable
rubrics_metrics.description: Suppose (B, n, k) is a regular local ring of dimension d. Let A := B[x]. Suppose p is a prime ideal of A such that nB[x] ⊂ p. Then A_p is a regular local ring.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Geometric proof: consider π : Spec B[x] → Spec B. Either p lies over n as the generic point of the fiber A1_k (case p = nB[x]) or p corresponds to a closed point of the fiber (given by a monic irreducible g(x)). Use Krull's Height Theorem and the fact that n is generated by d elements to compute heights and show pA_p is generated by d (resp. d+1) elements, hence regular. This proposition is used to show that X×A^1 is regular when X is regular.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regularity preserved under product with A1 (exercise / consequence)
rubrics_metrics.description: If X is a regular (locally Noetherian) scheme, then so is X × A^1. In particular, A^n_k is regular.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Proposition 12.3.6 to check regularity at primes lying over maximal ideals; the argument reduces to local computations as in the proposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of dual projective space
rubrics_metrics.description: The dual (or dual projective space) to P^n_k (with coordinates x0,...,xn) is the projective space P^n_k with coordinates a0,...,an (denoted P^n∨_k) together with the incidence correspondence; k-points of P^n∨_k correspond to hyperplanes in P^n_k cut out by a0 x0 + ... + an xn = 0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This concrete coordinate description suffices for many applications and extends over arbitrary bases (e.g., Spec Z). One may formulate a coordinate-free definition if desired.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bertini's Theorem (12.4.2)
rubrics_metrics.description: Suppose k = k̄ (algebraically closed) and X ⊂ P^n_k is a smooth subvariety. Then there is a nonempty (dense) open subset U of the dual projective space P^n∨_k such that for any closed point [H] ∈ U which does not contain any component of X, the scheme H ∩ X is k-smooth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bertini is often used to show existence of a single hyperplane H with smooth intersection. 'General' means a closed point of U. Variants (e.g., Kleiman-Bertini) exist; characteristic hypotheses may be needed for refined statements (see Exercises 25.3.D/E).

rubrics_metrics.name: Bad hyperplanes form a proper closed subset (proof strategy for Bertini)
rubrics_metrics.description: Define Z ⊂ X × P^n∨ as the locus of pairs (p,H) where p ∈ X ∩ H and either p is a singular point of H ∩ X or H contains X. The projection π: Z → P^n∨ has image a closed subset of dimension ≤ n−1, so its complement is a nonempty open subset of 'good' hyperplanes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compute fibers W_p (hyperplanes containing p for which H ∩ X is singular at p or contains X); these impose d+1 linear conditions when dim X = d, so fibers have dimension n − d − 1, and apply dimension-counting (Key Exercise 11.4.A) to bound dim Z ≤ n − 1.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jacobian criterion for regularity and for constructing Z
rubrics_metrics.description: The Jacobian matrix of defining equations for X has corank equal to dim X at all closed points of X (Jacobian criterion). For the incidence Z one appends the column (a0,...,an) and requires that the augmented Jacobian have corank ≥ dim X + 1 at (p,H) (i.e., certain minors vanish) to encode singularity of H ∩ X at p.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is encoded by polynomial equations (determinants of minors), so Z is a closed subscheme. Example 12.4.4 (plane conic) illustrates computing the augmented Jacobian and recovering tangent lines.

rubrics_metrics.name: General hyperplane intersections yield reduced finite sets (12.4.C)
rubrics_metrics.description: If X ⊂ P^m is projective of dimension n and degree d, then the intersection of X with n general hyperplanes consists of a finite number of reduced points: there is a Zariski-open U ⊂ (P^m∨)^n such that for each closed point (H1,...,Hn) of U, the scheme-theoretic intersection H1 ∩ ... ∩ Hn ∩ X is a finite reduced set.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assume k algebraically closed for convenience; this is a standard Bertini-type application and gives classical enumerative consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dual variety and properties (12.4.5)
rubrics_metrics.description: The image of Z in P^n∨ is called the dual variety of X. Since dim Z = n − 1, one expects the dual to be a hypersurface of P^n∨; classically, the dual of the dual of X is X itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This construction links tangency conditions and projective duality; exercises give examples (e.g., dual of a smooth conic is a smooth conic).

rubrics_metrics.name: Discrete valuation: definition and valuation ring
rubrics_metrics.description: A discrete valuation on a field K is a surjective homomorphism v: K^× → Z satisfying v(x+y) ≥ min(v(x), v(y)) unless x+y = 0. Extend by v(0)=∞. The valuation ring Ov := {x ∈ K : v(x) ≥ 0} is a local ring; its unique maximal ideal is {x : v(x) > 0}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Key examples: (i) 5-adic valuation on Q; (ii) power of x valuation on K = k(x); (iii) negative-degree valuation on k(x). Not every valuation is discrete (e.g., valuations to Q for Puiseux series).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of discrete valuation ring (DVR)
rubrics_metrics.description: An integral domain A is a discrete valuation ring if there exists a discrete valuation v on its fraction field K such that Ov = A.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equivalently: A is a Noetherian regular local ring of dimension 1; the valuation gives a uniformizer t with every nonzero element uniquely u t^n (u unit, n ∈ Z). Exercises show converses (if A is DVR then it is Noetherian regular local of dim 1, and vice versa).

rubrics_metrics.name: Equivalent characterizations of 1-dimensional Noetherian regular local rings / DVRs (12.5.1, 12.5.4, 12.5.6, 12.5.8)
rubrics_metrics.description: Suppose (A,m) is a Noetherian local ring of dimension 1. The following are equivalent: (a) A is regular; (b) m is principal; (c) all ideals are of the form m^n (n ≥ 0) or (0); (d) A is a principal ideal domain (exercise); (e) A is a discrete valuation ring; (f) A is a unique factorization domain; (g) A is integrally closed in its fraction field.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proofs show the chain of implications and converses: regular ↔ m principal ↔ ideal-structure condition ↔ DVR ↔ UFD ↔ integrally closed. Use Nakayama, Krull's Principal Ideal Theorem, and valuation constructions to move between these forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Valuation from uniformizer and uniqueness
rubrics_metrics.description: If (A,m) is a Noetherian regular local ring of dimension 1 with uniformizer t, any nonzero element r of A can be written r = u t^n with u unit and n ≥ 0; extend to K(A)^× as u t^n for n ∈ Z defining v(ut^n) = n. On a DVR there is a unique discrete valuation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This constructs the discrete valuation and shows uniqueness; exercises ask to check that v satisfies valuation axioms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Orders of zeros and poles at regular codimension-1 points
rubrics_metrics.description: For a locally Noetherian scheme X, any regular codimension-1 point p (so O_{X,p} is a DVR) yields a discrete valuation v on the fraction field. For any nonzero f in the fraction field, v(f) > 0 means f has a zero of order v(f) at p; v(f) < 0 means a pole of order −v(f).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This formalizes zeros/poles of rational functions on schemes, and exercises (12.5.G) show zeros/poles are finite in number on integral Noetherian schemes. If a rational function has no poles, it is regular (Algebraic Hartogs's Lemma 11.3.10 / exercise 12.5.H).

rubrics_metrics.name: Dedekind domain localization and ideal factorization (12.5.14)
rubrics_metrics.description: A Dedekind domain is a Noetherian integrally closed domain of dimension ≤ 1. Localization at any nonzero prime (i.e., codimension-1 prime) yields a discrete valuation ring. Every nonzero ideal in a Dedekind domain factors uniquely as a product of prime ideals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rings of integers in number fields are examples. Exercises show special cases (e.g., certain quadratic integer rings) and the unique ideal factorization property.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structure theorem for finitely generated modules over a DVR (12.5.15)
rubrics_metrics.description: Any finitely generated module over a DVR A (with uniformizer t) is a finite direct sum of cyclic modules of form A and A/(t^r) for various r.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is analogous to the structure theorem over PIDs and is used for later consequences (see Proposition 13.7.3).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of smooth morphism (12.6.2) and étale morphism
rubrics_metrics.description: A morphism π: X → Y is smooth of relative dimension n if there exist open covers {U_i} of X and {V_i} of Y with π(U_i) ⊂ V_i and diagrams U_i ≅ W → Spec B where W is an open subscheme of Spec B[x1,...,x_{n+r}]/(f1,...,fr) with the property that at every point of W the determinant det(∂f_j/∂x_i)_{i,j≤r} is an invertible function on W. Étale means smooth of relative dimension 0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: From the definition smooth morphisms are locally of finite presentation. Examples: projection A^n_B → Spec B is smooth of relative dimension n; open embeddings are étale. The definition is chosen to be workable despite seeming unmotivated; later chapters give more conceptual formulations. Exercises cover base change, composition (relative dimensions add), openness of smooth locus, and local factorization as an étale map followed by projection (12.6.B–12.6.E).

rubrics_metrics.name: Key properties/exercises about smooth and étale morphisms
rubrics_metrics.description: Smoothness is local on source and target, preserved by base change, composition adds relative dimensions (if π is smooth of relative dimension n and ρ is smooth of m then composite is smooth of m+n), smooth locus is open, and locally a smooth morphism factors as an étale map to A^n over the target.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are the fundamental closure and local properties that make the class of smooth/étale morphisms 'reasonable' (see Exercises 12.6.B–12.6.F). They justify treating smooth morphisms as a robust geometric notion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equivalence of k-smooth definitions for k-schemes (12.6.3)
rubrics_metrics.description: For a k-scheme X the following are equivalent: (i) X is smooth of relative dimension n over Spec k (Definition 12.6.2); (ii) X has pure dimension n and is smooth over k in the sense of the earlier definition (Definition 12.2.6).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The equivalence is a key compatibility check: the local Jacobian corank condition in the afffine presentation matches the earlier notion of smoothness over a field. The proof reduces to local algebra and uses Krull's Principal Ideal Theorem and Jacobian/tangent-space computations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Valuative criteria motivation (prelude to §12.7)
rubrics_metrics.description: In reasonable circumstances one can verify separatedness (and properness) by checking only maps from spectra of valuation rings: this gives intuition about separated morphisms, fits the Yoneda viewpoint of understanding objects by maps into them, and one direction of the valuative criterion is easy and frequently used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The valuative criteria use discrete valuation rings; §12.7 will make this precise and provide statements for separatedness and properness. This section is placed after DVR theory because of this dependence.
